prompt.context: Your client is an entrepreneur looking to invest in a new bar. He needs to determine how profitable the company will be and convince his primary investor, his father, that it will be a viable business.
prompt.question: What factors would you consider and investigate?

clarifying_info.q: What does the average customer spend on food per visit?
What does the average customer spend on drinks per visit?
What are the gross margins for food and drinks?
clarifying_info.a: Food has a 20% gross margin; drinks have a 50% gross margin
Kitchen: 4 people at $10/hr. Bar: 1 person at $5/hr. Wait staff: 3 people at $5/hr.

clarifying_info.q: How many customers does the bar expect per hour?
clarifying_info.a: Sunday-Wednesday day (12pm-8pm): 10 food customers/hr and 4 drink customers/hr. Sunday-Wednesday night (8pm-12am): 4 food customers/hr and 15 drink customers/hr. Thursday-Saturday day (12pm-8pm): 15 food customers/hr and 5 drink customers/hr. Thursday-Saturday night (8pm-2am): 5 food customers/hr and 20 drink customers/hr.
There is no specific data on utilities, legal, insurance, licenses, training, remodeling, equipment, and other startup costs.

framework: Revenues: food revenue and drinks revenue, driven by customer traffic (volume) and spend per visit
Costs: COGS (food and drinks), labor (kitchen, bar, wait staff), lease, and other operating costs (utilities, marketing, insurance, licenses, startup costs)
Profitability: weekly and annual profit = revenue minus COGS minus labor minus lease
Investment viability: break-even period and ROI relative to alternative investments for the father

questions.prompt: Calculate total weekly orders for food and drinks.
questions.guidance: Candidate should systematically build a table: day hours x customers/hr = daytime orders, night hours x customers/hr = night orders, sum for daily orders, multiply by days per week, then sum food and drink weekly totals.

math.setup: Split by Sun-Wed (4 days) and Thu-Sat (3 days); split by food and drinks; split by day (12pm-8pm = 8hrs) and night (Sun-Wed 8pm-12am = 4hrs; Thu-Sat 8pm-2am = 6hrs).
steps: Sun-Wed food: day = 10 x 8 = 80, night = 4 x 4 = 16, daily = 96, weekly = 96 x 4 = 384
Sun-Wed drinks: day = 4 x 8 = 32, night = 15 x 4 = 60, daily = 92, weekly = 92 x 4 = 368
Thu-Sat food: day = 15 x 8 = 120, night = 5 x 6 = 30, daily = 150, weekly = 150 x 3 = 450
Thu-Sat drinks: day = 5 x 8 = 40, night = 20 x 6 = 120, daily = 160, weekly = 160 x 3 = 480
math.answer: 834 weekly food orders; 848 weekly drink orders

questions.prompt: Calculate weekly revenue and weekly COGS for food and drinks.
questions.guidance: Multiply weekly orders by price per order to get revenue. Apply COGS percentages (food 80% of revenue; drinks 50% of revenue) to get weekly COGS.

math.setup: Revenue = orders x price per order. COGS = revenue x (1 - gross margin). Food gross margin 20% means COGS = 80% of food revenue. Drinks gross margin 50% means COGS = 50% of drinks revenue.

questions.guidance: Compute total hours for each role across the week (Sun-Wed and Thu-Sat), then multiply by hourly rate and headcount.

math.setup: Kitchen and bar and wait staff are staffed whenever the bar is open. Sun-Wed: 4 days x 12 hours (12pm-12am) = 48 hours. Thu-Sat: 3 days x 14 hours (12pm-2am) = 42 hours. Total hours per person = 90.
steps: Wait staff: 3 people x $5/hr x 90 hrs = $1,350

questions.guidance: Weekly profit = revenue minus COGS minus labor minus weekly lease. Convert to annual by multiplying by weeks per year.

math.setup: Weekly lease = $10,000/month divided by 4 weeks = $2,500/week. Assume 50 operating weeks per year.

questions.prompt: Given $500K in start-up capital, how long until break-even and what is the 5-year ROI?
questions.guidance: Break-even = up-front cost divided by annual profit. 5-year ROI = (annual profit x 5 years minus up-front costs) divided by up-front costs. Candidate should note this ROI is very low relative to alternative investments and the payback period is nearly the full 5 years.

math.setup: Up-front costs = $500,000. Annual profit = $104,100 (previously calculated). Assume no interest.
math.answer: Break-even in approximately 4.8 years; 5-year ROI = 4.1% (less than 1% per year)

brainstorming.prompt: What other factors and risks should be considered when advising the client's father on whether to invest?

categories.name: Revenue enhancement opportunities
ideas: Different operating model emphasis (food-heavy vs. drinks-heavy)

categories.name: Cost reduction strategies
ideas: Purchase used equipment to reduce startup costs

categories.name: External risks
ideas: Sudden rise in COGS (e.g., food shortage)
Decrease in customers after initial opening period

recommendation: From a financial perspective, the sports bar is projected to be profitable with annual profit of approximately $104K, but the break-even period of nearly 5 years and a 5-year ROI of only 4.1% (less than 1% annually) are very modest relative to the $500K initial investment.
The recommendation to the father should acknowledge long-term viability but strongly emphasize comparing this investment to alternatives with faster payback and higher returns.
risks: Several cost categories (utilities, marketing, insurance, licenses, remodeling, equipment) are excluded from this analysis and will reduce actual profitability when included
Location is a critical factor in determining foot traffic and competitive positioning that has not been quantified
COGS could rise unexpectedly due to supply chain issues or food shortages
Minimum wage increases could significantly raise the labor cost base
Customer volumes may decline after the novelty of opening wears off
next_steps: Incorporate utilities, marketing, insurance, and other excluded costs into the profitability model to get a more complete picture
Benchmark the projected ROI against alternative investments available to the father (e.g., index funds, real estate)
Investigate ways to reduce startup capital requirements (used equipment, phased renovation) to shorten the break-even period
Explore additional revenue streams such as events, advertising, or jukebox to improve margins
Conduct location analysis and competitive benchmarking to validate customer traffic assumptions
